items.readable_text:
Content:
Let's consider an equilateral triangle with sides of length [MATH: 2x]. Notice that any altitude will split it into two congruent triangles, as shown below.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/dc29a4c2d4070d598292198a22c2e694]

Content:
In the new smaller triangle the acute angles will be [MATH: 30^\circ] and [MATH: 60^\circ.] Such triangles are called [MATH: \boldsymbol{30^\circ}]-[MATH: \boldsymbol{60^\circ}]-[MATH: \boldsymbol{90^\circ}] triangles.

Content:
Based on the picture above, we see a special property shared by all [MATH: 30^\circ]-[MATH: 60^\circ]-[MATH: 90^\circ] triangles:

Content:
> In any [MATH: {30^\circ}]-[MATH: {60^\circ}]-[MATH: {90^\circ}] triangle, the hypotenuse is twice as long as the shortest leg (which is opposite the [MATH: 30^\circ] angle).

Content:
This also works in the other direction:

Content:
> If the hypotenuse is twice as long as the shortest leg, then the given right triangle is a [MATH: {30^\circ}]-[MATH: {60^\circ}]-[MATH: {90^\circ}] triangle.

Consider the same [MATH: {30^\circ}]-[MATH: {60^\circ}]-[MATH: {90^\circ}] triangle from before. This time, however, we will focus on the height ([MATH: h]) instead of the hypotenuse.

Applying the Pythagorean Theorem, we have

Content:
[MATH: (2x)^{2}|= x^{2} + h^{2}; h^{2}|= 4x^{2} − x^{2}; h^{2}|= 3x^{2}; h|= sqrt(3)x,]
which gives us the second important property:

> In any [MATH: {30^\circ}]-[MATH: {60^\circ}]-[MATH: {90^\circ}] triangle, the length of the longer leg (which is opposite the [MATH: 60^\circ] angle) is [MATH: \sqrt{3}] times the length of the shorter leg (which is opposite the [MATH: 30^\circ] angle).

Let's refer to our standard [MATH: 30^\circ]-[MATH: 60^\circ]-[MATH: 90^\circ] triangle.

Since this is a [MATH: 30^\circ]-[MATH: 60^\circ]-[MATH: 90^\circ] triangle, the length of the longer leg is [MATH: \sqrt{3}] times that of the shorter leg.

Here, the longer leg has length [MATH: 2,] and the shorter leg has length [MATH: x,] so we have

[MATH: 2|= sqrt(3)x; x|= (2)/(sqrt(3)).]

To remove the radical from the denominator, we can multiply the numerator and denominator by the radical:

[MATH: x|= (2)/(sqrt(3)) = (2 ⋅ sqrt(3))/(sqrt(3) ⋅ sqrt(3)) = (2sqrt(3))/(3)]

So, the length of the shorter leg is [MATH: \dfrac{2 \sqrt{3}}{3}.]

Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:
Let's consider an equilateral triangle with sides of length [MATH: 2x]. Notice that any altitude will split it into two congruent triangles, as shown below.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/dc29a4c2d4070d598292198a22c2e694]

In the new smaller triangle the acute angles will be [MATH: 30^\circ] and [MATH: 60^\circ.] Such triangles are called [MATH: \boldsymbol{30^\circ}]-[MATH: \boldsymbol{60^\circ}]-[MATH: \boldsymbol{90^\circ}] triangles.

Content:
Based on the picture above, we see a special property shared by all [MATH: 30^\circ]-[MATH: 60^\circ]-[MATH: 90^\circ] triangles:

Content:
> In any [MATH: {30^\circ}]-[MATH: {60^\circ}]-[MATH: {90^\circ}] triangle, the hypotenuse is twice as long as the shortest leg (which is opposite the [MATH: 30^\circ] angle).

Content:
This also works in the other direction:

Content:
> If the hypotenuse is twice as long as the shortest leg, then the given right triangle is a [MATH: {30^\circ}]-[MATH: {60^\circ}]-[MATH: {90^\circ}] triangle.

[MATH: \sqrt{3}x = \sqrt{3} \cdot 3 = 3\sqrt{3}.]
